stimulus.text: The engraving, 'The Bloody Massacre perpetrated in King-Street Boston on March 5th 1770,' was engraved, printed, and sold by Paul Revere. It shows a neat line of British soldiers firing a single volley into a crowd of Bostonians, with five men fallen in the foreground. Below the image, the names of the dead are listed: Samuel Gray, Samuel Maverick, James Caldwell, Crispus Attucks, and Patrick Carr — 'Killed. Six wounded.'
stimulus.source_note: Paul Revere, 1770. Library of Congress. Public domain (pre-1930).

books.section: A. Colonial Resistance to British Policies in the Aftermath of the French and Indian War
The Sugar Act, the Currency Act, and the Stamp Act

stem: The engraving presents the soldiers as...

options.text: Fleeing from an armed colonial militia
options.misconception: No militia is shown, and the soldiers are not fleeing — they stand in a neat firing line, which is the point of the image.

options.text: Defending themselves against a surprise attack
options.misconception: The engraving shows no attack on the soldiers — the crowd is unarmed and falling, while the soldiers fire in order.

options.text: Refusing an order to fire on the crowd
options.misconception: The soldiers are shown firing, not refusing — the image's charge is that they fired deliberately, on command.

options.text: Firing a deliberate, ordered volley into an unarmed crowd

rationales.D: Look at the line: the soldiers stand shoulder to shoulder, muskets level, firing together through one cloud of smoke. The engraving shows a deliberate volley, not a scramble — that is the charge it makes.
rationales.A: There is no militia and no flight. The soldiers advance in formation; the crowd falls.
rationales.B: No attack on the soldiers is shown. The crowd is unarmed, and the soldiers fire in order.
rationales.C: The soldiers are firing, not refusing. The image's accusation is that they fired on command.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the soldiers first. They stand in a neat line, muskets level, firing as one — the image of an ordered volley.
2. Look at the crowd. Men fall in the foreground, unarmed, with no weapons shown in their hands.
3. Ask what the picture argues. Not that shots were fired — everyone agreed on that — but that the firing was deliberate murder, ordered and carried out.
Remember: an image can argue as loudly as a paragraph — read the arrangement, not just the subject.
